To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Poisson(1), which is a proper discrete prior, can serve as the prior for the number of mixture components k, that the hyperparameter values for the mixture model can be chosen in a way that is both simple and effective, and that the Gibbs sampling technique can be used for the posterior computation of the parameters of the mixture.

(1) the Poisson(1), rather than the Poisson(0), distribution should be used as the prior on the number of components, and that (2) the hyperparameter values for the normal components of the mixture should be chosen to be equal.
the Poisson(1)-prior for k, the method of moments for selecting the hyperparameters, and the Gibbs sampling algorithm for computing the posterior distribution of k, are all effective.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the specification of prior distributions in the context of a Bayesian analysis of finite mixture models.
a Bayesian approach to finite mixture problems and with the development of a computational method that is applicable to a wide class of mixture models.
the following issues: prior specification; computation of the marginal likelihood; and posterior computation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the method of the present article should be considered for use as the default method for the analysis of finite mixtures.

the Bayesian finite mixture model is a very attractive approach to the analysis of mixture data, with the proviso that a careful choice of the prior specification and the computation method is required.
the Bayesian approach is the most natural way to deal with the mixture problem, and that the methods proposed here can be used in a wide range of applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the new method for the posterior computation is a very efficient and accurate algorithm for the computation of a posterior distribution for k, and that the Poisson(1)-prior is a good choice of prior for the number of mixture components.
the Poisson prior for k, with a Gamma(1, 1) prior for the mixing proportion, is a natural and useful choice for the mixture of normals problem.

, for the mixture of normals case, the use of a prior for the number of components that is Poisson(1), and the use of a mixture of normal priors with equal variances for the component means, are reasonable choices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when using natural conjugate pri ors, it is important to select the hyperparameter values carefully, as the posterior distribution of k is highly sensitive to the choice of these values.

the Poisson(1)-Dirichlet prior for the number of mixture components is an excellent choice for the analysis of finite mixture models, as it is easy to implement and leads to a very simple posterior distribution.
, in the absence of prior knowledge on the number of components, it is preferable to use a non-informative prior for k, such as the Poisson(1).
